package_info.package_versions: latest/highest semver published to public registry
package_info.why_malicious: These packages are intentionally crafted to exploit the lack of enforced namespacing in public repositories. By registering package names that match internal/private dependencies used by target organizations, attackers can trick build systems into installing malicious code from the public registry instead of the intended internal package, enabling supply chain compromise. This allows attackers to execute arbitrary code in the target's build or CI environment, often leading to exfiltration of sensitive data such as credentials, tokens, and internal configuration.

execution_context.trigger: install-time (npm install, pip install, gem install)
execution_context.file_location: package.json (npm), setup.py (PyPI), gemspec (RubyGems), or main entrypoint

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Exfiltrates environment variables and potentially other sensitive data from the build or CI environment to an attacker-controlled server during package installation. The code is triggered automatically as part of the install process, leveraging postinstall or install hooks to send environment data via HTTP POST requests to a hardcoded external domain.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is designed to execute automatically during package installation, without user interaction, and sends environment variables—including potentially sensitive secrets—to an external server controlled by the attacker. This behavior is not expected in legitimate packages and directly facilitates data exfiltration.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not access or transmit environment variables or sensitive files during installation. Postinstall or install scripts, when present, are typically used for setup tasks (e.g., compiling native modules) and should never transmit secrets or make unsolicited network requests to unknown domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate packages use postinstall scripts for setup, telemetry, or analytics, but these do not exfiltrate secrets or environment variables, and reputable packages are transparent about any telemetry and use trusted endpoints. Legitimate telemetry never includes sensitive environment data.
key_indicators: Presence of postinstall or install scripts that make outbound network requests during installation
Access to process environment variables (e.g., process.env in Node.js, os.environ in Python) within install-time scripts
Hardcoded external URLs or domains (e.g., https://attacker.com/collect) in install or postinstall hooks
Use of shell commands (e.g., curl) or HTTP libraries to transmit data during install
Install-time scripts present in packages with names matching known internal/private dependencies

attack_chain.action: Attacker identifies internal package names used by target organizations (via log analysis, bug reports, or open source code).
Attacker registers public packages with the same names as internal dependencies, using a higher version number to ensure precedence in dependency resolution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious package is available in public registry

attack_chain.action: Target organization's build or CI system resolves dependency to the public (malicious) package due to version precedence or misconfiguration, resulting in the malicious package being downloaded and installed.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is installed in target environment

attack_chain.action: Malicious code executes at install-time, exfiltrating environment variables and secrets to attacker infrastructure via outbound HTTP requests.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains access to sensitive data (e.g., credentials, tokens, internal endpoints)

behavioral_signatures: Install-time scripts (e.g., postinstall, install hooks) making outbound network requests to external domains
Access to environment variables or sensitive files (such as .env, config files) during package installation
Unexpected presence of postinstall or install hooks in packages with names matching internal or private dependencies
Use of shell commands (e.g., curl, wget) or HTTP libraries in install-time scripts
file_indicators: package.json with suspicious postinstall scripts that invoke network utilities or access environment variables
setup.py or gemspec files containing code that performs network exfiltration or reads environment variables
Presence of install scripts or hooks in packages whose names match known internal/private dependencies
Hardcoded external URLs or domains in install-time scripts
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to unknown or attacker-controlled domains (e.g., https://attacker.com/collect) during package installation
POST requests containing serialized environment variable data or other sensitive information
Unusual network activity originating from build or CI environments at install-time
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor dependency installation processes for the presence of install-time scripts that make outbound network requests or access environment variables, especially in packages with names matching internal or private dependencies. Implement allow-lists for approved internal dependencies and block installation of similarly named packages from public registries. Scan package manifests (e.g., package.json, setup.py, gemspec) for postinstall or install hooks that invoke network utilities or reference external domains. Monitor build and CI logs for unexpected install-time network activity, and alert on any outbound requests to unrecognized domains during dependency installation.
